title: Labneh with za'atar and olive oil
subtitle: Strained yoghurt with dried herb blend
excerpt: Labneh with za'atar is strained Greek yoghurt served cold, drizzled with good olive oil and a generous scatter of the dried herb mix. It takes two minutes to assemble and is the easiest thing to put on a mezze table.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Labneh and za'atar described as an everyday breakfast and mezze staple across Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Labneh keeps in the fridge for up to five days. Add the za'atar and oil just before serving.

content.text: Labneh is strained yoghurt: thick, creamy, and slightly tangy, halfway between yoghurt and soft cheese. Spread on a plate and covered with za'atar and good olive oil, it needs nothing else. The za'atar blend adds dried thyme, sumac, and sesame; the olive oil binds it into something almost sauce-like at the edges.
Use the best olive oil you have here; it is the main flavour alongside the za'atar. Pitta bread or flatbread alongside for scooping.
Season {{greek-yoghurt}} lightly with sea salt and stir together. Spread it in a wide, shallow pool on a plate or in a shallow bowl, using the back of a spoon to make a thin well in the centre.
Drizzle {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} over the surface, letting it pool in the centre.
Scatter {{za-atar}} generously over the top. Add olives if using. Serve at once with warm bread.

items.symptom: The labneh is too loose to spread neatly
items.cause: Greek yoghurt brands vary in thickness
items.fix: Line a sieve with muslin or a clean tea towel and leave the yoghurt to drain over a bowl in the fridge for two hours. It will thicken considerably.

items.symptom: The za'atar tastes dusty rather than fragrant
items.fix: Buy a fresh batch. Za'atar loses its oils quickly after opening. Store in a sealed jar away from light.

items.symptom: The dish looks flat on the plate
items.cause: Too little olive oil or za'atar
items.fix: Be generous with both. The za'atar should form a visible crust over the surface, not a dusting.

items.cause: Very thick or extra-strained yoghurt can be quite tangy
items.fix: Stir a teaspoon of honey through the yoghurt before spreading. It softens the acidity without making it sweet.

content.text: Labneh with za'atar is the most common breakfast plate in Lebanon, served alongside sliced tomatoes, olives, eggs, and flatbread. The za'atar mix itself is treated almost as a condiment in Levantine households: a jar of it sits on the table the way pepper sits on a British one. Thyme, sumac, and sesame are the core, but the ratios vary by family and region. Syrian versions tend to have more sumac; Palestinian versions more thyme. The dish is also common in Jordan and Israel, where it appears at breakfast buffets and home tables alike.
